opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a great question, because I think people often assume that since I came out of neuroevolution, I must be some kind of biological purist. And actually I'm not. I don't place much importance on fidelity for its own sake. What I care about is fidelity to the *principles* that seem to matter, not to the details of how nature happened to implement them.

Take something like CPPNs, the compositional pattern-producing networks we used in Picbreeder and later in HyperNEAT. They're inspired by developmental biology. In embryos you have things like gradients and symmetric, repeating structures that get established through a kind of coordinate frame. But a CPPN doesn't simulate chemicals diffusing through a cell, there's no physics of morphogens. It just composes functions like sines and Gaussians and gets the same *kind* of regularity: symmetry, repetition, repetition with variation. That abstraction turned out to be enough to capture what I think is the important part.

And what's really interesting, and this is what Picbreeder taught me, is that the representations that came out of that system were remarkably well-organized. If you found a skull image and perturbed the network, you'd get the jaw opening and closing, or the eyes getting bigger, as if the network had some kind of understanding of what a skull is. It wasn't because we were faithful to biology. It was because of the *process* that produced those networks. People weren't optimizing toward the skull. They were wandering, following stepping stones that seemed interesting. The skull was discovered, not targeted.

So if I were to say where biological fidelity really matters, it's less in the low-level mechanisms and more in the nature of the search process itself. Evolution in nature is not an objective optimizer in the way we usually think of it. It's open-ended. It's divergent. It keeps accumulating stepping stones and branching off into new niches. That's the deep lesson I'd want to preserve. And I suspect that's connected to why natural representations are so elegant and so reusable, as opposed to what I'd call fractured, entangled representations that you often get when you just hammer on an objective with gradient descent. They may perform, but underneath they can be kind of a mess.

So, short answer: I'm happy to throw away the biology as long as I keep the parts that seem to explain why nature's stuff is so good. And I'd say the open-ended, non-objective character of the process is high on that list, probably higher than any specific mechanism.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he does not value biological fidelity for its own sake and is willing to discard biological details while preserving useful principles, so faithful modeling is not required to produce good representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Not that much, honestly. I'm not trying to replicate biology. What I care about is the underlying principle that makes evolution work, not the specific mechanism nature happened to use. Nature is a kind of existence proof. It shows you that an open-ended process with no objective can produce staggeringly elegant representations, from the structure of a brain to the regularities in a body plan. But the details of how DNA does it, or how recombination works in sexual reproduction, those are incidental. They are one solution to the problem of building a representation that can keep getting more complex and more interesting over time.

So when I built things like NEAT or HyperNEAT or CPPNs, I borrowed the abstraction, not the implementation. The idea of complexification, starting simple and gradually adding structure, that's inspired by how evolution actually elaborated genomes over billions of years. The idea of indirect encoding, where a compact genome unfolds into a much larger phenotype through a developmental process, that's clearly biological in spirit. But a CPPN is not a model of embryogenesis. It's a compositional abstraction of what development buys you: symmetry, repetition, repetition with variation. If I had tried to be faithful to chemistry and gene regulatory networks I think I'd have gotten lost in the weeds and never gotten the insight.

The thing that interests me most, and this is where the fidelity question gets interesting in a different way, is that representation and search are entangled. In nature, you don't get nice representations because something was optimizing for niceness. You get them because the search is open-ended, it's divergent, and representations that are modular and regular happen to be the ones that keep being viable as things get elaborated over a long time. A tangled, fragile encoding doesn't survive thousands of steps of further elaboration. So the elegance is almost a side effect of the kind of process that produced it. That's a principle I do want to take seriously, and it's actually why I've drifted away from objective-driven optimization in general, including in deep learning.

And you can see the difference. When you train a network with gradient descent on an objective, you tend to get what I've called fractured entangled representations. They work, they get the right answer, but inside they're a mess, with the same concept split across weird disconnected regions. Whereas when you look at networks produced by something like Picbreeder, where humans were just following their curiosity through a divergent search, the representations are strikingly unified. A symmetric face has an actual symmetry parameter you can turn. That contrast is more informative to me than any amount of biological fidelity. It tells me the process matters, not the fact that it was carbon-based.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it is not trying to replicate biology and values evolution’s underlying principle rather than nature’s specific mechanisms, directly stating that good representations do not require faithful biological modeling.

astra-6.text:
I think biology is incredibly useful as a source of ideas, but fidelity to biology isn’t really the goal for me. The question is which aspects of evolution are responsible for its creativity, and which are incidental to the particular way life happens to be implemented on Earth.

If you’re interested in representations, one of the striking things about biology is that the description of an organism isn’t a separate instruction for every little piece of it. There’s a developmental process that produces structure, with regularities and repetitions and variations on those repetitions. That suggests something useful computationally: a representation can make certain kinds of organized complexity easy to discover. We don’t necessarily need to reproduce all the biological machinery to capture that idea.

But there’s a danger in simplifying, too. You can remove something that looks like an inconvenient detail and accidentally remove the thing that makes the process powerful. So I’d want to understand what a biological feature is doing, then ask whether we can preserve that function in a simpler system. Ultimately, I care more about capturing the principles that allow evolution to keep producing interesting things than about making a simulation that looks biologically realistic.

r001.rationale: The candidate says fidelity to biology is not the goal and that the biological machinery need not be reproduced to capture useful principles for representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think biology is incredibly useful as a source of inspiration, but I don’t think fidelity to biology is the objective. The question is which aspects of evolution are doing the work that we care about. You can abstract away a lot of the details and still capture something important, and sometimes the abstraction actually makes the principle easier to see.

For me, one of the most interesting things about evolution is that it produces representations without being told what those representations should ultimately be useful for. It wasn’t trying to invent human intelligence. So if we build a system where every change is judged by whether it gets closer to a particular outcome, we may have left out something quite fundamental, even if other parts of the system look biologically realistic.

So I’d put more emphasis on capturing those kinds of principles than on reproducing every biological mechanism. Ultimately, you have to test whether the abstraction gives you the kind of richness and capacity for discovery that you’re looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says biological fidelity is not the objective and that important evolutionary principles can be captured while abstracting away many biological details.
